articles.title: The Cord Anyone Could Pull
articles.dek: A failing California car factory didn't fire its workers to fix itself — it handed them a rope and told them to pull it the moment something looked wrong. Paul tells a jumpy young church something just as strange: you don't need to know the hour, only whose side of the clock you already stand on.
articles.quote: You don't stay alert because you're afraid of the dark. You belong to the morning, so you already know how to watch for it.
articles.body:
In 1982, General Motors closed its Fremont, California plant and called it the worst in the company. Absenteeism ran so high that managers sometimes couldn't field enough workers to start the line. Cars left the factory with bottles rattling inside their doors, deliberately sealed in by employees who'd stopped caring. Nobody expected the place to reopen.

Then Toyota did something strange. In 1984, it partnered with GM to reopen the plant as NUMMI, rehired nearly the same union workforce — the one everybody had already written off — and gave every single worker on the line a rope. Literally. A cord hanging above each station, called the andon cord, that any worker could pull the instant they spotted a defect. Pulling it didn't just flag a problem. It stopped the entire line. A team leader would rush over immediately, no blame, just help. Within months, the exact same people who'd been sealing bottles into doors out of spite were producing some of the highest-quality cars in North America. Nothing about the workforce had changed. What changed was this: they were no longer asked to work and hope nobody noticed the flaws. They were trusted — and expected — to stay awake to them.

Paul is writing to a church in Thessalonica that is wide awake with the wrong kind of alertness. They're anxious, asking about times and dates — exactly when the Lord will return, exactly when the clock runs out (1 Thessalonians 5:1). It's the posture of someone straining to catch a supervisor before he catches them. Paul doesn't play along. "You know very well that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night," he says (5:2) — suddenly, unannounced, while people are busy saying "peace and safety" (5:3), confident the line is running fine, right up until it isn't.

But then he turns, and the turn is everything. "You, brothers and sisters, are not in darkness so that this day should surprise you like a thief" (5:4). Not because they'd cracked the schedule. Because of what they already were: "You are all children of the light and children of the day. We do not belong to the night or to the darkness" (5:5).

So then, let us not be like others, who are asleep, but let us be awake and sober. (1 Thessalonians 5:6, NIV)

Here's what's easy to miss on a first read: Paul never tells them to stay awake so they won't get caught. He tells them to stay awake because they're already children of the day — people who belong to the morning don't need to fear what the night hides. Vigilance, in this passage, isn't dread wearing a disguise. It's identity working itself out. The NUMMI worker who pulled the cord wasn't terrified of getting fired. He'd been told, repeatedly, that noticing the flaw was exactly what he was there for. That's a different engine than fear entirely, and it runs longer without burning out.

Paul even describes the gear for staying awake, and it's worth noticing what kind of gear it is. "Since we belong to the day, let us be self-controlled, putting on faith and love as a breastplate, and the hope of salvation as a helmet" (5:8). A breastplate guards the chest — the heart, the most exposed and vulnerable part of a person. A helmet guards the head — where a person decides whether to keep going or give up. Faith and love over the heart. Hope over the mind. This isn't armor for attacking anything. It's armor for enduring a long watch without going numb or going hard.

And watches, it turns out, were never meant to be kept alone. Paul doesn't end the thought with the individual believer standing guard in isolation. The very next line is: "Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing" (5:11). At NUMMI, the cord worked because the whole floor was trained to respond to it — a team leader ran toward the problem, not away from the person who raised it. A lone worker pulling a cord that nobody answered would have just been shouting into a silent factory. The system only held because everyone on it had agreed to notice together.

Read the rest of Paul's closing instructions with that in mind and they stop sounding like a scattered list of good manners: comfort the discouraged, help the weak, be patient with everyone, don't repay wrong for wrong, rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances, do not quench the Spirit (5:14–19). These are small cords, hung all over a community, each one within reach of ordinary hands. Nobody has to carry the whole watch by themselves. Somebody just has to be willing to pull, and somebody else has to be willing to come running when they do.

So here's a question worth sitting with this week: where is your cord hanging, and have you told anyone they're allowed to pull it? Maybe it's a friend who needs permission to say "something's wrong" before it becomes a crisis. Maybe you're the one who's spotted a small defect in someone you love — a withdrawal, a silence, a joke that isn't quite a joke — and politeness has been talking you out of saying anything. Paul's whole point is that the Thessalonians didn't need to calculate the hour. They needed only to remember whose they already were, awake, armored, and never watching alone. You don't stay alert because you're afraid of the dark. You belong to the morning, so you already know how to watch for it. Find one person today and be, for them, the hand that answers when the cord is pulled.

articles.title: The Tree They Almost Threw Away
articles.dek: A charred, broken pear tree pulled from Ground Zero still blooms every spring — and Jeremiah says the difference between surviving and withering was never the weather.
articles.quote: Roots dug in the middle of a drought are roots dug too late.
articles.body:
In October 2001, recovery workers combing the ruins of the World Trade Center found something nobody expected to survive. Wedged in the rubble near a parking lot was a tree. It was a Callery pear, maybe eight feet tall, and it was in terrible shape. Its trunk was split and charred black. Its roots had been snapped and torn, half of them exposed to the air. Every branch was broken except one, which still held a few green leaves. Workers were clearing debris by the truckload. Someone almost sent the tree away with the rest of the wreckage.

Someone else said wait.

The New York City Parks Department took the tree to a nursery in the Bronx and started over with it. It was not a quick fix. For nine years, staff nursed that battered root ball back to health, and it was not a straight road. A storm once tore the tree out of the ground entirely, days before it was scheduled to be moved. They had to cut it back hard and start the healing again. Nobody outside that nursery saw any of it. There was no blossom to photograph. Just years of quiet work on roots nobody could see.

In the fall of 2010, the tree went home. It was replanted at the National September 11 Memorial, right among the new saplings surrounding the two reflecting pools, and it earned a name: the Survivor Tree. Today it is usually the first tree in that whole plaza to bloom each spring, its white flowers opening before any of its younger neighbors even bud. And since 2013, the Memorial has grown seedlings from its seeds and given them away, one at a time, to communities that have survived their own tragedies — the finish line in Boston, a school in Newtown, a nightclub in Orlando, places on nearly every continent. Each sapling arrives with the same quiet message: something broken this badly grew roots deep enough to flower again, and so can what grew from it.

Jeremiah would have understood that tree.

By the time we reach chapter 16, Jeremiah has been told to do strange, public things — no wife, no funerals to attend, no parties to join — so that his whole life becomes a sign to Judah of the devastation coming. The nation had built its confidence on alliances, on idols, on its own cleverness, on anything but God, and Jeremiah is watching that confidence come apart in real time. Chapter 17 opens with an indictment: their sin is engraved on their hearts "with a flint point, on the tablets of their hearts" (Jer 17:1). Then, a few verses later, comes the line so many people know without knowing where it is from: "The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. Who can understand it?" (Jer 17:9). It is not a flattering diagnosis. But it sets up one of the most quietly beautiful passages in the whole book.

God, through Jeremiah, draws two trees.

"Cursed is the one who trusts in man, who draws strength from mere flesh and whose heart turns away from the LORD," he says. "That person will be like a bush in the wastelands; they will not see prosperity when it comes. They will dwell in the parched places of the desert, in a salt land where no one lives" (Jer 17:5-6). It is a brutal little picture — a shrub clinging to cracked, salted ground, never quite dying, never quite living either, missing every good thing even when it finally arrives.

Then the other tree.

"But blessed is the one who trusts in the LORD, whose confidence is in him. They will be like a tree planted by the water that sends out its roots by the stream. It does not fear when heat comes; its leaves are always green. It has no worries in a year of drought and never fails to bear fruit." (Jer 17:7-8)

Here is the detail worth sitting with: the blessed tree is not exempt from heat. It is not spared the drought. Verse 8 says the heat comes. It says the drought year arrives. The difference between the two trees was never the weather. Both trees stand in the same hard country. The difference is what is happening underground, out of sight, long before anyone can see it — roots "sent out by the stream," reaching past the dry surface toward a water source the eye cannot find from where it's standing.

That is exactly what nobody could see while the Survivor Tree sat in that Bronx nursery for nine quiet years. From the outside, there was nothing to look at — a damaged trunk, slow progress, a setback or two. The actual healing, the part that mattered, was happening underground the whole time, in roots reaching toward water that hadn't been visible since the morning it was pulled from the rubble.

This is where Jeremiah's wisdom turns relational, because the test he describes is really a test of where we send our roots when life gets hard. "Trusts in man" and "draws strength from mere flesh" are not condemnations of friendship or family — Scripture elsewhere delights in both. They describe making another person, your own resourcefulness, your reputation, or your bank account the water table you quietly depend on to get you through. All of those sources are good gifts. None of them are bottomless. Flesh tires. People disappoint, even the ones who love you most. Plans fail. And when the drought comes — and Jeremiah assumes it will come, for both trees — whatever you've rooted yourself in gets exposed.

It's worth asking, plainly: in the dry season you're in right now, where are your roots actually reaching? Toward a person who is also running on empty? Toward your own grip and hustle, which is already tired? Or toward the stream that Jeremiah says never runs dry, even in a salt land?

None of this means the heat won't come. It means you get to choose, today, where the roots go looking for water before the heat arrives — because roots dug in the middle of a drought are roots dug too late. That's a decision made in ordinary, unremarkable days: time in his word, honest prayer, people who point you back to him instead of only to themselves. Quiet, underground work that nobody applauds, the kind that was happening in a Bronx nursery long before anyone saw a single white blossom.

And maybe the most hopeful part of the whole story is what happened after the Survivor Tree finally recovered. It didn't just bloom for itself. Its seedlings have been carried to the exact kinds of places Jeremiah pictures — parched, salted, grieving ground — as proof that something can come back from that. Whatever drought you're walking through right now, roots sent deep enough won't just keep you standing. One day it may be the very thing you hand to someone else still waiting for their own rain.

articles.title: The King Who Was Told to Sit
articles.dek: Before any battle in Psalm 110 begins, the coming King is given a strange first command: sit down. A quiet discovery about sleeping brains shows why that's not the same as giving up.
articles.quote: For some battles, rest at the Father's side is how the fight gets won.
articles.body:
In 2012, a neuroscientist named Maiken Nedergaard made a discovery that overturned decades of textbook certainty about the brain. For as long as anyone could remember, the brain was thought to be the one organ in the body without its own dedicated cleaning system — no lymph channels to flush out the metabolic debris that builds up from a day's worth of thinking, remembering, and feeling. Every other organ had a way to take out its trash. The brain, somehow, did not, and scientists had wondered for a century why that gap even mattered.

Nedergaard's team found the truth was stranger, and better, than that. The brain does have a cleaning system — it just only switches on while you are asleep. A study her lab published in the journal Science in 2013 found that during deep sleep, the spaces between brain cells widen by roughly sixty percent. Cerebrospinal fluid rushes into those newly opened channels and washes out the toxic proteins that accumulated during waking hours, including amyloid-beta, the protein tangled up in Alzheimer's disease. Part of the answer to why we need to sleep at all turns out to be this: your brain cannot do its most important defensive work while you are awake, alert, and striving. It can only do it while you are still.

Psalm 110 opens on a throne, and it begins with that same quiet surprise.

This is a short psalm, only seven verses, but no verse in the entire Old Testament is echoed in the New Testament more often. Jesus himself quotes its opening line in the temple courts, cornering the religious leaders who are trying to trap him with questions (Matthew 22:41–45). The LORD declared to my Lord, David writes — meaning this is a king writing about a King greater than himself, a coronation oracle aimed past his own throne toward someone still to come.

Picture David composing it. He has fought his whole life. Goliath. Saul's spear. Years hiding in caves and wilderness, then years of armies, betrayal, his own son's rebellion. David knows exactly what it costs to win and hold a throne — every inch of his own kingdom was paid for in exhaustion. In the royal courts of the ancient Near East, the seat at a king's right hand was the most coveted place in the kingdom, reserved for a trusted co-regent, not a soldier. So when David sits down to write about the greater King who is coming, we would expect him to reach for the language he knows best: chariots, swords, the roar of battle. For a moment he does — verse 3 pictures troops volunteering on the day of battle, verse 2 pictures a scepter extending out from Zion. This is a real war psalm.

But the very first line is not a command to fight. It is a word spoken by the LORD to David's Lord — Yahweh speaking to the Messiah.

"The LORD says to my Lord: 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.'" (Psalm 110:1, NIV)

Sit. Before any sword is drawn in this psalm, before any battle is even described, the King is told to take a seat. Not just any seat — the right hand, the place of highest honor beside the throne itself, the position reserved for the one closest to the Father's own heart.

Here is what is worth noticing. The enemies in verse 1 are not yet defeated. The footstool has not yet been made. The war, if anything, is still underway — that is what the word until tells us. And yet the King's own posture, in the middle of an unfinished war, is not clenched fists or a braced stance. It is sitting. The hardest, most decisive work being done against the enemies in this verse is not being done by the Son's own exertion at all. It is being done by the Father — until I make your enemies a footstool. The Son's part, astonishingly, is simply to rest in the place closest to the one doing the work.

That is not what we expect rest to mean. We tend to think of rest as what happens after the war is won — the medal ceremony, not the battlefield. But Psalm 110 pictures something close to what Nedergaard found in sleeping brains: the fiercest defensive work sometimes only happens in the posture of stillness. The King does not sit because the fight is over. The King sits, and the sitting is somehow part of how the fight gets won.

A few verses later, the psalm adds one more detail about this King: You are a priest forever, in the order of Melchizedek (Psalm 110:4). Melchizedek appears only once before this, in Genesis 14 — a king and priest with no recorded beginning and no recorded end, who simply blesses Abraham and disappears from the story. It is a strange, quiet credential to hand the coming King. Not a record of battles won, but a record of belonging near God long before any war began. The writer of Hebrews would later lean on this exact verse to describe a King whose priesthood never ends, and who therefore always lives to intercede for those who come to him (Hebrews 7:24–25). The resting and the interceding, it turns out, are the same posture.

Maybe you know the feeling of trying to win a battle your hands were never built to fight: a wayward adult child you cannot control, a diagnosis you cannot out-plan, a conflict at work that no amount of your own striving will resolve, a grief that will not move no matter how hard you push against it. Or something smaller but just as wearing — a hospital corridor at midnight, a phone that will not ring with the answer you need, a form that has been sitting on someone else's desk for weeks. The instinct, in all of these, is to grip tighter. Do more. Stay alert every waking hour as if your own vigilance is the only thing holding the line.

Psalm 110 offers a different instinct. It invites you to the seat at the right hand — not the front line, not the command post, but the place closest to the Father, where your part is nearness rather than exertion. This does not erase your part entirely — verse 3 still pictures willing troops, verse 2 still pictures a scepter doing real work in the world. But the psalm insists on starting with sit, not stand and fight, because it wants you to know where the decisive power actually comes from before it asks anything of your hands.

Rest is not only what you do when the fight is over. For some battles, rest at the Father's side is how the fight gets won.

There is an intimacy in this worth lingering over. Sit at my right hand is not a throne across the room. It is a seat beside him — close enough to feel his nearness, close enough that the posture itself is a kind of embrace. The psalm is not only describing authority. It is describing closeness. Before Jesus is pictured ruling anything, he is pictured sitting beside his Father, near enough to belong there.

So today, if there is a battle you have been standing up straight to fight with your own strength, try something smaller first. Just for a few minutes, actually sit down with it instead. Not giving up on it, but bringing it to the seat at the right hand, and leaving it there a while — the way your own brain leaves its worst debris behind each night, trusting someone else to do in the stillness what you never could have done awake. That is a seat worth keeping, long after today ends.

articles.title: The Hill They Built Before They Needed It
articles.dek: Proverbs spends four verses on the storms we cause with our own mouths — and then names a refuge none of us ever had to build.
articles.quote: The tower was already standing before the storm had a name — all the righteous have to do is run.
articles.illustration: Dutch terp mounds against North Sea floods
articles.body:
In the flat, windswept lowlands of what is now the Netherlands, Frisian farmers faced a problem no fence could solve. More than two thousand years before anyone built a modern dike, the North Sea had no respect for property lines. When a storm pushed a surge inland across the marsh, the water did not trickle in. It arrived like a wall, swallowing fields, barns, and homes within hours. So these farmers did something quietly brilliant. They built hills. Not natural ones, hand-built ones, raised basket of earth by basket of earth, generation after generation, until whole villages sat on artificial mounds called terpen, some rising thirty feet above the surrounding marsh. Houses, livestock pens, grain stores, all set on top. Today you can still see them dotting the Frisian countryside, round green hills with farmhouses on them, looking for all the world like ordinary hills until you learn that human hands raised every one of them, load by load, long before anyone living today was born. One of the oldest, at Hogebeintum, has been lived on continuously since before the time of Christ. When the surge came, as it reliably did, water spread for miles across the lowland, and the terp, with the entire village still standing dry on it, rose out of the flood like an island.

Here is what is worth noticing. The terp was never something villagers scrambled to build once the sky turned black. By the time the storm arrived, the work was already finished, decades finished, sometimes centuries finished. Nobody debated the floor plan at two in the morning while water lapped at the door. There was nothing left to decide. You simply ran, up the slope, children in your arms, animals ahead of you, and you were safe. The safety had not been negotiated in the moment of crisis. It had been prepared long before anyone needed it, by people who understood exactly how desperate that moment would one day be.

Filipinos know this instinct without needing an explanation. Every barangay near the coast has an evacuation center on a rise of ground, marked with a sign long before any storm forms out at sea. Nobody waits for the water to start climbing the steps before deciding where safety is. The decision was already made, posted, and practiced, months or years earlier. That is exactly the kind of foresight Solomon has in mind two verses later, except the tower he describes was never built by any committee at all.

Solomon knew a different kind of flood, the one we cause ourselves. Proverbs 18 opens with a string of warnings about exactly this, and they are worth reading together, because they build like rising water.

"The lips of fools bring them strife, and their mouths invite a beating," he writes. "The mouths of fools are their undoing, and their lips are a snare to their very lives" (Proverbs 18:6–7). Then he names a particular kind of careless speech, gossip, and makes an uncomfortable observation about why it spreads so easily: "The words of a gossip are like choice morsels; they go down to the inmost parts" (Proverbs 18:8). Gossip is not just overheard. It is savored, like a good meal. That is why it travels so fast through a family group chat or an office pantry. It tastes good going down, even while it is doing damage underneath. Solomon adds one more flood of our own making: "One who is slack in his work is brother to one who destroys" (Proverbs 18:9). Four verses, four ways of flooding your own life, careless words, self-destructive words, gossip, laziness. Every one of them a storm with no one else's fingerprints on it but yours.

And then, without warning, Solomon turns from the flood to the refuge.

"The name of the LORD is a fortified tower; the righteous run to it and are safe." (Proverbs 18:10)

Here is the turn worth sitting with. The terp had to be built by human hands, generation after generation, before anyone could run to it. But the tower in verse 10 is not something the righteous construct. It is not a tower of our own careful words, our own reputation, our own hard-won credibility, all of which verses 6 through 9 just showed us how easily we demolish ourselves. It is the name of the Lord, already strong, already standing, already finished, long before this morning's quarrel or this afternoon's rumor ever started. The Hebrew phrase behind "fortified tower," migdal oz, literally means a tower of strength, the same kind of structure a whole town would retreat to when an enemy broke through the outer walls. It was never meant to be stylish. It was meant to still be standing when everything else had fallen. Notice too how simple the verb is. The righteous run. Not negotiate, not deliberate, not first make sure they have earned shelter. They just run, the way a Frisian farmer ran at the first sign of rising water, without stopping to ask whether he deserved the high ground he had not built himself.

This matters on an ordinary Friday, because most of our storms look exactly like verses 6 through 9. Someone says something careless about you in a group chat, and the old reflex is to answer with sharper words of your own, reinforcing a flood with more of the same water. A rumor reaches you, tasting as good as Solomon warned it would, and the temptation is to pass it on just one more time. A deadline slips because you let something slide, and now you are scrambling to defend yourself instead of simply owning it. Or a relative forwards a rumor about someone working overseas, and before anyone checks whether it is even true, it has already done damage three provinces away. In every one of those moments, there is a tower already standing, finished long before the trouble started. It does not ask you to win the argument first. It does not ask you to be in the right before you come. It only asks you to run.

So here is something small to carry into today, the next time careless words, yours or someone else's, start rising around you like that first dark line of water on the horizon. Before you answer, before you forward it, before you defend yourself, say the name quietly, even just in your own head. Lord. That is the whole first step. Not a magic word, but a reorientation, a reminder that the tower was already standing before the storm had a name — all the righteous have to do is run.
